From: Requester <[redacted]>
Date: Mon, 9 Feb 2026 10:27:08 -0300
Subject: Requester . Nec Vi, Nec Clam, Nec Precario - Heir & Successor to Williams/ Buckler Dynasty, Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan
Message-ID: <CAAuJ3V6OByMKHZhie+pE28Y-HK-tWVmMkXgkHuHaDZjA+Chv5A@mail.gmail.com>

Sirs / Ma’am,

I write from the Welsh settlement in Patagonia, Argentina, with respect,
and for the attention of His Majesty King Charles III and the appropriate
officers of the Royal Household.

I write as a Welsh national, a father, and a former public servant. I
concluded twenty-two years in oath in 2024, including a career in the
military, also serving in the Middle East and leaving colour service with
honours. I recently completed employment under the Welsh Government (Vale
of Glamorgan Council). I now write in a private capacity, not under oath,
and not in any adversarial posture, but in good faith and with the
intention that the historic record be accurately preserved.

My purpose in writing is to place on record serious concerns regarding the
historical treatment, documentation, and subsequent erasure of my family’s
ancestral estate, Tŷ Mawr (Great House Farm), Llandough, in the Vale of
Glamorgan.

Tŷ Mawr was an historic monastic grange and site of Roman antiquity. From
1667, it was held in continuous occupation and stewardship by my fathers
sides maternal family, the Williams family, later intersecting with the
Buckler line through marriage. For over three centuries, my forebears
occupied, worked, and maintained this land. I was born there.

Prior to enlisting in Signals Intelligence roles and encountering senior
national and royal figures in the course of official duties, I was educated
in Wales, including at Llandovery College, which I attended under the
Government-run Assisted Places Scheme, having been selected on academic
merit. On my mothers side, my late grandfather, the Welsh BAFTA-winning
actor Ray Smith, carried the same Welsh cultural identity into public life.
My wider family has likewise contributed to Welsh cultural life, including
my aunt Shan Cothi, the opera singer, and her husband/ my late uncle;
Justin Smith, founder of the Welsh band Tigertailz and directed a major
'visit wales' campaign for the tourist board. These details are to
demonstrate continuity of Welsh cultural life rooted in this family and
place. I'm also a fluent speak Welsh, I named my daugher Delyth, and I do
much for the continuity of Welsh cultural life.

In 1974, my grandmother on my fathers side; Mary Williams, initiated
proceedings concerning the title to Tŷ Mawr. Those proceedings were
adjourned and later that same year effectively extinguished without
substantive resolution. Critically, my grandmother never adopted her
husband’s surname; she remained Mary Williams throughout her life. That
name was not incidental. It was the living link to the 1667 acquisition of
the farm and to our family’s long occupation.

During later proceedings, the name “Mrs Buckler” was ascribed to her in
court records. This misidentification had material consequences. It severed
the documentary continuity of the Williams line and undermined both our de
facto occupation and any consideration of adverse possession. This
misnaming remains, to my knowledge, uncorrected in the public record.

In 1988, my family was forcibly removed from Tŷ Mawr, having been
characterised as squatters despite centuries of occupation. Our home — an
800-year-old farmhouse — was demolished shortly thereafter. I was four
years old. I witnessed the destruction alongside my siblings and parents.
We were not permitted to retrieve belongings or family records. Centuries
of family material history were lost.

Of particular concern is that the site had long been associated with Roman
remains. In 1870, a Roman burial was reportedly uncovered on the land, a
fact later omitted or minimised in official descriptions of the site.
Following the demolition of the farmhouse, and prior to residential
development, it emerged that the land contained what is now understood to
be the largest Roman burial site excavated in Wales, with over 1,000
burials. Had this been properly recorded and acknowledged earlier,
statutory archaeological protections should have applied.

The effect of these events has been the near-total erasure of the historic
and indigenous Welsh continuity of Tŷ Mawr from public narrative and
record. The land now forms part of a modern housing development, without
acknowledgment of its significance or of the family that occupied it for
over three centuries.

I wish to be clear: my primary concern is not confrontation, but correction
— correction of the historical record, acknowledgment of documented
irregularities, and preservation of truth for future generations. My family
has carried the consequences of these events for decades, including
significant trauma, and many remain reluctant to come forward.

I hold a forensic analysis estimating the financial losses associated with
Tŷ Mawr at approximately £101.2 million, but the greater matter is not
monetary. It is the restoration of narrative accuracy and the
acknowledgment of indigenous Welsh continuity at this site and my families
standing in our local community thereafter. The generational trauma is so
deep, even last week my mother refused to discuss this, even privately.

I do not write to demand action from His Majesty personally, nor do I
presume upon the Crown. I write so that it cannot later be said that these
matters were unknown or unrecorded. I respectfully request that this
correspondence be retained as a notice of concern regarding historic record
integrity, misidentification of parties, and the suppression or omission of
material archaeological and cultural facts.

My intention is also to rebuild an exact replica of Great House Farm in
Patagonia, where the Welsh community here has welcomed the preservation of
this history. This project is intended as an act of cultural conservation,
not protest.

I remain respectful of the Crown’s constitutional role and of the King
personally. My request is simply that the truth of Tŷ Mawr — its history,
its people, and its erasure — is not allowed to disappear entirely from the
historical record.

I certify that I write in good faith, with full mental capacity, and
without hostility. I seek only truth, acknowledgment, and preservation of
history.

Yours faithfully,

Sion Hywel Buckler
[redacted], Wales
[redacted]

From: Requester <[redacted]>
Date: Tue, 10 Feb 2026 19:15:25 -0300
Subject: Formal Notice for Record: Church View Close, Llandough / BP vs Buckler 1987
Message-ID: <CAAuJ3V4Cf9dTUEsGhwQQYD2W+YrO+3hc9eTZ27jf4+OHrtZQBw@mail.gmail.com>

*FORMAL NOTICE OF RECORD CHALLENGE, ASSERTION OF RIGHT, AND DEMAND FOR
ENGAGEMENT*

Dear Sir/Madam,

This Notice is issued for placement on official record and for reliance. It
is not informal correspondence. I urge you not to resort to silence,
deflection, or delay, as doing so following receipt of this notice
constitutes knowing reliance upon, and maintenance of, records alleged to
be materially defective through fraud, concealment, denial of due process,
and systemic erasure. Please report any suspicious activity and
discrepancies identified.

This Notice is issued in pursuit of narrative justice at this stage; formal
judicial remedies are expressly reserved. It serves to document our
family's side of the story before it is completely erased and history
rewritten, ensuring awareness among custodians of land, heritage, heraldry,
archaeology, and public records.

My elder brother, Rhys Buckler, and I are the sons of the late William
Buckler (d. 1991), defendant in the landmark legal case *BP Properties Ltd
v Buckler* (1987), and the grandchildren of the late Mary Williams, whose
dispossession, marginalisation, and exclusion from judicial determination
remain unresolved matters of record. Mary Williams was repeatedly and
materially falsely addressed/mislabeled in legal and administrative records
as “Mrs Buckler,” a misidentification that was never judicially tested and
which directly affected the handling, scope, and outcome of proceedings.
The Williams/Buckler family held claim to the land title, having acquired
and occupied Great House Farm continuously since 1667, based on family
records, historical evidence, and centuries of resistance to adverse claims.

I place on record that I am the first member of my family able to speak
publicly and formally on these matters. Other close family members remain
too traumatised and intimidated by the historical conduct of these
proceedings—including violent eviction, demolition, and loss of
livelihood—to engage, despite the continuing consequences of dispossession.
That silence must not be misread as consent, acquiescence, or abandonment
of right. There is a material distinction between free silence and silence
produced by fear, trauma, and coercive experience.

The story, as we have pieced it together, reveals a multi-generational
pattern of lawfare and siege: from Norman/English conquests in 1100
granting lordships over ancient Welsh Christian landscapes, through
monastic (1215–1539) and Crown seizures (1539 onward), to industrial
encroachments (e.g., 1876 Limeworks severance without consent) and modern
corporate possession actions. This culminated in the 1988 demolition of an
800-year-old farmhouse amid police standoffs, leaving the family homeless
and the site scarred, now buried under Church View Close. Archaeological
vindication came too late—1994 excavations revealed over 1,000 Roman and
medieval burials, confirming family warnings (e.g., the 1870 Roman soldier
discovery under the living room floor, suppressed by authorities)—yet
heritage records celebrate the site while omitting our dispossession.

The following assertions of right are now formally placed on record. They
have never been lawfully adjudicated or extinguished:

   1. Rhys Buckler may be the rightful Manorial Lord of the Manor of
   Llandough, by right of primogeniture and continuous hereditary connection
   arising from our family’s occupation of Great House Farm from 1667 until
   our narrative, legal, and physical dispossession.
   2. I assert a claim to act as Squire of the Manor of Llandough, as
   executive representative and guardian of the Buckler–Williams estate and
   matriarchal lineage, with a mandate to pursue correction of record,
   restitution, and restorative remedies.

These are assertions of right, not settled declarations, placed on record
pending proper adjudication—which has been historically obstructed through
procedural narrowing, missing documents, and avoidance of full hearings.

In 1974, Mary Williams was twice prevented from presenting her case and
obtaining a judicial determination of superior ownership, despite claims
grounded in long occupation, intent, and possession. The court confined
inquiry to *animus possidendi* (intention to possess) and excluded *animus
domini* (intention to own), reclassifying her from putative owner to mere
occupier and foreclosing title adjudication. BP sought possession only, not
ownership rulings—a choice unexplained and significant. Proceedings were
adjourned or quashed without resolution.

This occurred despite evidence of ownership intent, including:

   - Centuries-long occupation and resistance (e.g., failed 1938 auction
   due to local support; post-1945 rent disputes).
   - Roman-era remains and historical significance (e.g., Guglielmo
   Marconi's 1897 residence during radio experiments, with family aid erased
   from records).
   - Unformalized deals like the 1895–1905 Daniel Thomas quarrying
   permission for promised title, undermined by vanished deeds.

Judicial ownership examination would have engaged archaeological/heritage
protections, incompatible with redevelopment—consequences avoided, raising
credibility concerns.

Serious unresolved anomalies persist, indicating something is still not
right with the record:

   - Licence correspondence dated 31 October 1974 surfacing only on 4
   November, potentially interrupting proceedings to prevent hearings.
   - Claims of 1974 benevolent withdrawal under press scrutiny unsupported
   by verifiable coverage.
   - Land registration before Mary Williams’s 1983 death without title
   determination; disputes possibly lodged/suppressed by Land Registry.
   - Inconsistent treatment of BP entities across proceedings to family
   detriment.
   - Procedural barriers preventing effective defense (e.g., interrupted
   essential services post-licence; 1960–1987 court rulings dismissing
   ancestral title as "notion" without evidence).
   - Knowing bypass of archaeological constraints (e.g., 1978 trenches
   ignored; no contemporaneous 1970s/1990s press on discoveries amid
   development).
   - Missing key documents (e.g., 1667 conveyance, 1811–1835 Lambert
   Williams agreements proving status, 1982–84 library deeds vanishing).
   - Risks of further erasure: Heritage databases celebrate "Llandough
   Roman villa cemetery" while omitting our saga; modern residents unaware of
   the "battleground" site.

These anomalies suggest systemic theft, from colonial English subjugation
(e.g., 1543–1770 orbit shifts) to corporate siege, during Wales'
cultural/economic transitions. Authority derived through such means is
illegitimate under natural justice, customary Welsh principles, and
moral-legal frameworks. The record's distortion secures advantage, but
passage of time does not validate it.

Preliminary assessment indicates cumulative benefits from redevelopment
(absent title extinguishment) exceed £100 million, forming a basis for
reparations—covering lost land, artifacts, livelihood, and trauma.

I require relevant public servants, custodians, and office-holders
(including Land Registry, heraldry bodies, museums, archaeologists, MPs,
historians, and councillors) to cease delay, engage substantively,
review/correct/annotate records where defective, and prevent further
rewriting of history. Justice delayed is denied, especially with verifiable
evidence available.

This Notice:

   - Challenges the record's accuracy, completeness, and legitimacy.
   - Place assertions of title/standing on record pending adjudication.
   - Reserves all rights without prejudice.
   - Puts officials/beneficiaries on notice that silence/reliance may
   aggravate responsibility.

For the avoidance of doubt, His Majesty the King was notified yesterday.

This serves as an invitation to engage constructively before reliance
becomes untenable.

Regards, Requester On behalf of the Buckler–Williams family [redacted], Wales. https://bpvsbuckler.datro.xyz

*Postscript — Disability and Succession (Material Notice):* The
heir-apparent to the asserted Manorial Lordship is Rhys Buckler’s son, a
young man with Down syndrome. Any obstruction, marginalisation, or
differential treatment affecting his inheritance would engage the Equality
Act 2010 and UK international obligations on disability rights. Disability
cannot bar succession or recognition. This is recorded to prevent claims of
ignorance.

That is a very fair point, Bob. You’re right to be cautious—sometimes a "hostile" tone can cause a civil servant to shut down or hide behind red tape rather than helping you.

The reason it feels like they are being cooperative is that they have shifted from saying "no" to asking for evidence. This is a good sign. However, the reason we are "rebutting" is simply to correct their premise: they think this is a recent fraud, and you are correcting them that the "fraud" was the original act of registration in 1982.

Let’s soften the tone to be "Helpful but Firm." We will treat them as an investigator who needs your guidance to find the truth, rather than an enemy.

Adjusted "Cooperative" Draft

Subject: Information regarding Registration Irregularities – Great House Farm (Ty Mawr) – Ref: 260202-5732372

Dear S.-G. Haste,

Thank you for your guidance on how to proceed with this report. I appreciate the opportunity to clarify the nature of the irregularities I have identified.

As requested, I have attached a detailed PDF timeline which provides the full address and the historical context of the land formerly known as Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough.

To assist your investigation into how the 1982 registration may have been affected by material non-disclosure, I would like to highlight three specific areas where the "actual facts" on the ground differed from the application made to the Registry:

  1.  Overriding Interests (The Williams Lineage): At the time of first registration in 1982, my family had been in continuous possession since 1667. I believe the registration was irregular because it misidentified the occupant, Mary Williams, as "Mrs. Buckler"—a name she did not use—effectively obscuring a 320-year "Living Title" from the Registry’s records.
  2.  Suppression of Material Facts (Archaeology): The site had "actual notice" of national archaeological significance due to a Roman discovery in 1888. I am concerned that this was suppressed during the registration and planning phases to facilitate the land's transition to housing.
  3.  Unresolved Ownership Claims: In 1982, there was an active, adjourned ownership dispute (from 1974) that I believe should have been disclosed to the Land Registry before a clean title was granted to BP Properties Ltd.

I am copying in the relevant heritage and oversight bodies (Cadw, GGAT, and the Ombudsman) not as an act of hostility, but to ensure that all parties holding pieces of this historical puzzle are aware that an investigation into the integrity of the 1982 registration is now underway.

I have also copied in my MP, the Senedd, and relevant heritage bodies to ensure that all parties with an interest in Welsh cultural heritage and public record integrity are kept informed as we look into these 1982 registration details.

I look forward to your thoughts on how we can review the original 1982 application files to see if these interests were disclosed.



Yours sincerely,



Sion Buckler

Descendant of the Williams family,

of Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough

Ms Smith,
Thank you for your detailed response regarding selection policies and retention schedules. I appreciate the procedural clarity you have provided. However, I must respectfully indicate that your reply does not address the substantive concerns I have raised, and I am now compelled to escalate this matter formally.
1. From "Archival Silence" to Potential Evidence Tampering
You correctly note that archival silences are well-documented in academic literature. However, the circumstances surrounding Great House Farm suggest something more concerning than routine selection decisions. I am now in possession of first-hand testimony (David Buckler, 2024) alleging that:

  *
Frederick Buckler (my grandfather) and his eldest son engaged a solicitor privately in the 1960s
  *
Title documents were removed from the family home and allegedly sold
  *
The family was deliberately misled with the phrase "it's all been dealt with legally"

This testimony, combined with the disappearance of the Bute Estate → Daniel Thomas deed index card from Cardiff Library (reported missing in 1984), suggests potential spoliation of evidence rather than routine archival selection. The question is no longer "why weren't records preserved?" but "were records deliberately removed to prejudice a 320-year possessory claim?"
2. The Computerised Records Question
You direct me to search your catalogue. I have done so. However, I now ask specifically:

  *
Does The National Archives hold any digitised or microfilmed copies of the Bute Estate records that might contain references to the Daniel Thomas quarrying agreement (circa 1895-1905) or the 1938 auction at the Bear Hotel?
  *
Are there any internal indices or finding aids (particularly from the 1970s-1980s) that might reference Great House Farm, Llandough, or the BP/Western Ground Rents acquisition records that are not reflected in the current online catalogue?

The 1994 archaeological excavation report (Cotswold Archaeological Trust) confirms the site's national significance. The absence of corresponding land transaction records from the same period is itself an anomaly requiring explanation.
3. The BP Corporate Records Question
You note that parties are generally responsible for maintaining their own records. However, BP Properties Ltd and BP Pension Trust Ltd were corporate entities with statutory filing obligations. I ask:

  *
Were any BP corporate records relating to land acquisition in South Glamorgan (1969-1988) selected for preservation under the Companies Act or as part of the public record?
  *
Has The National Archives ever received or sought records from BP regarding the Great House Farm acquisition, demolition, or the 1987 litigation?

The Court of Appeal judgment [1987] EWCA Civ 2 notes that BP issued letters on 31 October 1974, not received until November 4th 1974 —letters that were allegedly "accepted by silence." The original correspondence would constitute primary evidence of potentially fraudulent misrepresentation. If these were not preserved, I ask under what authority they were destroyed and whether this occurred before or after the litigation concluded.
4. Request for Formal Investigation
I am not seeking annotation of records. I am seeking:

  1.
A formal review of whether records relating to Great House Farm, Llandough (ST 168 733) were selected for preservation, destroyed, or remain non accessioned;
  2.
A search of microfilm, digitised, or legacy finding aid holdings for any reference to the 1938 auction, Western Ground Rents acquisition, or the Daniel Thomas quarrying agreement;
  3.
Confirmation of whether The National Archives has ever received complaints regarding missing Bute Estate records or BP land acquisition documents from other researchers;
  4.
Guidance on the appropriate authority to investigate allegations of document removal from Cardiff Library (1984) and potential fraud in the 1982 land registration.

5. Public Interest and Parliamentary Scrutiny
This matter involves:

  *
The forced removal of a family from land occupied since at least 1667
  *
Demolition of a medieval structure described as a "dilapidated utility building" to avoid heritage protection
  *
Archaeological discoveries (1888, 1994) that were known but officially "forgotten"
  *
A Court of Appeal decision ([1987] EWCA Civ 2) that may have relied on incomplete or fraudulent evidence

I am copying my MP and the Parliamentary Ombudsman in this correspondence. I will also be submitting a Subject Access Request to HM Land Registry regarding the 1982 registration and a complaint to the Information Commissioner's Office regarding potential destruction of records relevant to ongoing property disputes.
I request a substantive response addressing the specific questions above within 20 working days. Should The National Archives be unable to assist further, I request a formal referral to the appropriate body with jurisdiction over historical record fraud and spoliation.
Yours sincerely,
Sion Buckler




On Sat, 7 Feb 2026 at 07:26, RESO Records Enquiries <RESORecordsEnquiries@nationalarchives.gov.uk<mailto:RESORecordsEnquiries@nationalarchives.gov.uk>> wrote:

Dear Requester,

The question about archival silences is one upon which there is a voluminous literature. Practically, however, the best way of making sense of what is and is not in the archives is to refer to the reports which shaped selection policies in the modern era - see especially the Report on Departmental Records (Cmnd 9136) and the Report on Legal Records (Cmnd 3084) - and the resulting retention and disposition schedules - see for example the one for the Court of Appeal (Civil Division) published here<https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/62b47cc9d3bf7f0affd65610/court-appeal-civil-division-rrds.pdf>.

What you will see from these is that the presumption for modern records is against permanent preservation. In general, apart from small samples to demonstrate the ordinary functioning of the courts/government departments, records are only preserved if they bear witness to moments of particular legal or policy significance or change. In the case of legal records, the presumption has been that parties would be responsible for maintaining their own records.

In terms of how to continue your search, my instinct is that you should consider exploring the holdings of the relevant local archive. You can also try some keyword searches in our catalogue - see, for example, these<https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/results/r?_d=PF%7CWORK%7CBD%7CHLG&_dss=range&_sd=1978&_ed=1988&_ps=60&_hb=tna&_srt=1&_q=archaeological+NOT+bill+NOT+%22PF+309%22> search results which highlight these<https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/results/r?_q=archaeological+NOT+bill+NOT+%22PF+309%22&_d=PF%7CWORK%7CBD%7CHLG&_dss=range&_sd=1978&_ed=1988&_ps=60&_hb=tna&_srt=1&_l=3> series as potentially a relevant source of desired information. You might also wish to search the registered files of the land registry in records series LAR 1<https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C10222>. You should be advised, however, that departmental records tend to focus more on policy than upon the treatment of individual cases.

I hope that this is helpful.

Yours sincerely,

Charlotte Smith﻿

Principal Records Specialist, Modern Legal Records
www.nationalarchives.gov.uk<http://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/>

Enquiry:



I note and appreciate your confirmation that the principal judicial series (J 157, J 83, J 84) contain no relevant material. Given the scale of the consequences flowing from the dispute—forced removal, demolition of an occupied dwelling, and loss of heritage fabric—the absence of supporting court or administrative files is itself significant for researchers.

Accordingly, I would be grateful for guidance on the following procedural points:

  *   how researchers are expected to interpret gaps or silence in the archival record where substantial actions plainly occurred;
  *   whether related non-judicial records (for example, departmental, planning, regulatory, or corporate records connected to land registration, planning consent, or archaeological works) are more likely to sit outside the obvious court series; and
  *   whether there is an appropriate mechanism for flagging concerns about record completeness or contextual risk, without seeking alteration of the records themselves.

For the avoidance of doubt, I am not alleging impropriety on the part of The National Archives or its staff. My concern is to ensure that the historical record is approached with appropriate caution where absence may unintentionally convey certainty or closure that did not exist at the time.

texts.wb-84e13bee:
From: Requester <[redacted]>
Date: Mon, 16 Feb 2026 14:31:46 -0300
Subject: Title Fraud and Procedural Concealment – Church View Close, Llandough (formerly Great House Farm/ "Ty Mawr")
Message-ID: <CAAuJ3V6c+iXa6gGoJzzbHDw13Xe_=baznjfVK902R-XwAzePZg@mail.gmail.com>

Councillor Carroll & co,

I write regarding potential gaps in the Council's planning and
record-keeping processes relating to Great House Farm, Llandough, which was
demolished in 1988 following the 1987 Court of Appeal decision in BP
Properties Ltd v Buckler.

Recent evidence suggests the Council may wish to examine its own position
on this matter, as it raises questions about procedural compliance and
record integrity that could expose the authority to wider scrutiny.

CORE ISSUES

**1. Identity and Procedural Integrity**

The 1987 judgment turned on a 1974 licence addressed to "Mrs Buckler". My
grandmother, Mary Williams, did not use or accept this designation.
Contemporaneous evidence (1978 newspaper article attached) records her
asserting ownership under her correct name.

If the 1987 court was not presented with this evidence, the judgment may
rest on an incomplete factual record. This raises procedural fairness
concerns relevant to any future review of the decision.

**2. Heritage Information and Statutory Compliance**

The site's archaeological significance was documented by 1978 (Roman
burials, monastic associations). Yet professional excavations in 1994
revealed 1,026 early medieval burials and monastic structures—findings that
should have prompted evaluation under the Ancient Monuments and
Archaeological Areas Act 1979.

Critical question: Did the Council conduct or require prior archaeological
assessment before granting permissions to demolish? If not, this represents
a potential gap in statutory process that may affect the validity of the
permissions granted.

**3. Land Registry Disclosure**

BP registered title in 1982 based on the disputed licence. The Council
should establish:
- Whether any dispute notice or heritage caution was lodged;
- Whether the Council disclosed relevant heritage information to the Land
Registry;
- What planning records exist from 1978–1988 regarding the site's known
archaeological potential.

**4. Corporate Identity Inconsistency**

During my father's appeal, the court treated BP Properties Ltd and BP
Pension Trust Ltd inconsistently—as separate entities when convenient, then
as one when dismissing his claim. This raises questions about how
thoroughly the litigation was scrutinised and whether the Council's records
reflect this uncertainty.

WHY THIS MATTERS TO THE COUNCIL

These issues go beyond a single historical dispute. They touch on:

- **Planning record integrity**: Whether heritage information was
adequately documented and acted upon;
- **Procedural compliance**: Whether statutory protections (Ancient
Monuments Act) were properly applied;
- **Institutional liability**: Whether decisions were made on incomplete or
misleading information;
- **Precedent risk**: Whether similar vulnerabilities may exist in other
historical planning decisions.

REQUESTS

I ask the Council to:

1. **Commission a review** of the planning permissions granted between
1978–1988 for Great House Farm, specifically examining what heritage and
archaeological information was available to decision-makers and how it was
handled.

2. **Refer this matter to the Monitoring Officer** for examination of
procedural compliance and record integrity.

3. **Establish** what correspondence, cautions, or dispute notices exist in
relation to this site's title or heritage status.

4. **Clarify the Council's current protocol** for handling historical title
disputes, previously unknown heritage information, or allegations of
material non-disclosure in past planning processes—to prevent recurrence.

I am not asking the Council to reverse the 1987 judgment or disturb current
residents. I am asking it to ensure its own records are accurate and its
own processes are defensible.

I attach the 1978 article and supporting documents, and am available to
meet or provide further information.

Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler, Sgt (Ret'd)
Executor for the Manor of Llandough

From: Requester <[redacted]>
Date: Tue, 17 Feb 2026 13:16:32 -0300
Subject: Re: Historic Adverse Possession Licence Interruption Case(s)
Message-ID: <CAAuJ3V5MgYu7R7f1UdNXShe2RJmXr-w3jRFnnrbZ5uZAdLoKvQ@mail.gmail.com>

Contact and Assessment Team,

Thank you for your email of 17 February 2026 outlining the Bar Standards
Board's role and reporting procedures.

Before submitting a formal report via your online form or other means, I
would appreciate any preliminary guidance the Board may be able to provide
on whether the matters I describe below appear to raise arguable issues of
professional conduct under the BSB Handbook that might merit further
consideration through your processes.

I write on behalf of my family in connection with the case BP Properties
Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2, which concerned a claim to adverse
possession of property at Great House Farm, Llandough (a historic site).
The Court of Appeal upheld the effectiveness of a unilateral licence
granted in 1974, finding that it ended the adverse nature of possession.

The concerns I wish to raise relate to the conduct of the barrister(s)
representing BP Properties Ltd in the 1987 proceedings, specifically:

1. Whether there was adequate consideration or challenge to the identity of
the addressee in the 1974 licence letters (addressed to "Mrs Buckler"),
given that the occupier was known as Mary Williams and did not formally
adopt the surname Buckler. She retained her maiden name Williams throughout
her life, as evidenced by her marriage records (married as Williams in
1936), court proceedings and dealings prior to 1974 (all referring to her
as Williams), and her 1983 death record (registered as Mary Williams). The
licence letters appear to be the first documents to use "Mrs Buckler," a
name which arguably carried no equivalent claim to the land as that held by
Mary Williams. This relates to whether the basis for the licence's
effectiveness was fully addressed in terms of offer/acceptance or meeting
of minds under relevant principles (e.g., as referenced in cases like Cundy
v Lindsay on consensus ad idem). The court's use of Latin phrases in the
judgment may not have fully reflected Mary Williams's actual superior land
claim.

2. Whether any relevant information concerning the property's heritage and
archaeological significance, or potential future demolition plans, was
known or should have been disclosed during the proceedings. The property
was a 13th-century monastic grange, and a Roman soldier in full armour was
discovered and reported by the family in 1870 beneath the farmhouse floor,
as emphasized in a 1978 newspaper article where Mary Williams stated, "This
is my house." The judgment was delivered on 31 July 1987, and the property
was demolished in December 1988 despite Cadw's active consideration of
emergency spot-listing. Subsequent archaeological excavations in 1994
confirmed the site as a major early-medieval monastic cemetery of national
importance, with over 800 burials.

3. Whether all material facts relating to the circumstances and addressing
of the 1974 licence letters were fully and properly presented to the court,
including any potential concealment or suppression of evidence regarding
the occupier's true identity, the 1667 family tradition of acquisition, or
the alleged 1984 removal of a key index card from Cardiff Central Library
that may have supported the family's ownership claim.

4. Whether the question of the family's potential superior title or
ownership — derived from centuries of occupation, the 1916 tenancy context,
and accumulated adverse possession — was adequately addressed or
challenged, given that possession proceedings may have deferred or avoided
a full determination of ultimate title.

5. Whether any assessments, surveys, or heritage-impact reports conducted
before the 1987 proceedings were fully disclosed, and if they addressed or
omitted historic reports of Roman and monastic burials on the site.

I understand that the Board cannot pre-determine the outcome of any
investigation and that complaints involving historical matters may involve
evidentiary challenges. However, I would be grateful for any indication as
to whether, on the face of the summarised issues and the attached document,
these appear to disclose potential breaches of the Handbook (e.g., duties
of candour, not to mislead the court, or integrity) that would justify
proceeding to a formal report.

This guidance would help ensure any subsequent submission is appropriately
focused and substantiated.

Thank you for your assistance. I look forward to your response.

Regards,

Sion Hywel Buckler Esq./Sgt (Ret'd)
of the Manor of Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan
On behalf of the family and The Restored House of Williams

Aelodau Anrhydeddus y Senedd,

Rwy’n ysgrifennu atoch i dynnu eich sylw at yr hyn yr wyf yn ei ystyried yn anghyfiawnder hanesyddol difrifol, yn ymwneud â’m teulu, y Bucklers, a dinistr Great House Farm yn Llandough — safle fferm a chartref o dros 800 mlynedd o hanes, gan gynnwys cysylltiadau mynachaidd a chysylltiad uniongyrchol â Guglielmo Marconi yn ystod datblygiad cynnar radio.

Mae’r mater hwn yn codi cwestiynau difrifol ynghylch hawliau tir, gweithdrefnau cyfreithiol, cofrestru tir, a hawliau dynol yng Nghymru.

Er enghraifft, mewn datganiad i’r wasg yn 1974, dywedodd fy nain yn gyhoeddus: “It’s my home.” Mae’r datganiad hwn, sydd yn fater o gofnod cyhoeddus, yn gwrth-ddweud yn uniongyrchol ganfyddiad Llys Apêl 1987 yn BP v Buckler, lle dywedwyd ei bod wedi bod yn “ddistaw” ac wedi derbyn trwydded BP a gyhoeddwyd yn 1974.

Yn yr un achos, gwrthodwyd apêl fy nhad ar y sail bod BP Pension Trust Ltd a BP Properties Ltd yn “effeithiol yr un cwmni”. Fodd bynnag, yn y dyfarniad yr oedd yn ei herio, nododd y barnwr nad oedd ymatebion fy nain i BP Pension Trust Ltd yn cyfrif gan mai BP Properties Ltd oedd yr hawlydd, ac mai cwmnïau ar wahân oeddent. Yn ymarferol, roedd hyn yn arwain at sefyllfa “pen y cwmni’n ennill, cynffon y teulu’n colli”.

Yn sgil hyn, cafodd fy nhad ei dynnu o’i wely ysbyty, ei garcharu heb gyhuddiad, a gosodwyd gorchymyn atal arno i’w atal rhag meddiannu ac amddiffyn ein fferm 800 oed rhag cael ei dymchwel. Cafodd ei gais i’r Llys Hawliau Dynol Ewropeaidd ei rwystro cyn iddo farw yn 1991, yn ddim ond 41 oed.

Ar y sail hon, rwy’n gofyn yn ffurfiol am Ddeiseb i sefydlu Ymchwiliad Cyhoeddus i’r achos hwn, fel mater o ddwyn tir hanesyddol ac o dorri hawliau dynol yng Nghymru.

Rwy’n weithiwr proffesiynol ym maes seiber a rhyfela electronig milwrol. Mae technolegau AI pwerus bellach ar gael i bob un ohonom, ac nid oes unrhyw reswm technegol pam na ellid archwilio’r mater hwn yn llawn ac yn drylwyr. Mae’r hyn a ddigwyddodd i’m teulu yn ymddangos fel anghyfiawnder dwys, aml-genhedlaethol, ac yn debyg i ffurf ar “lawfare”, lle y trinwyd fy nheulu fel llafur di-dâl i gynnal ased tir hyd nes yr oedd yn gyfleus i’w ariannu. Mae’n arwyddocaol bod bron pob cam yn ein herbyn wedi digwydd ar yr eiliad olaf posibl.

Ceir honiadau bod sylw sylweddol yn y wasg yn 1974 o blaid fy nain a’n teulu, ynghyd â deiseb o tua 1,700 o bobl yn ceisio atal dymchwel y fferm. Ymhellach, mae’n ymddangos bod CADW wedi methu ag ymyrryd lle dylai’r safle fod wedi cael statws Adeilad Rhestredig Gradd II.

Nid wyf yn sicr a gofnodwyd erioed yn briodol yn y Gofrestrfa Tir fod y tir — a gofrestrwyd gan BP yn 1982 — dan anghydfod. Yn fy nealltwriaeth i, cafodd ei drin fel pe na bai mewn anghydfod o gwbl. Nid oes unrhyw lys wedi penderfynu’n derfynol mai BP oedd perchnogion cyfreithiol y tir; cafodd hynny ei honni yn hytrach na’i brofi.

Mae hefyd fater pwysig o hanes diwylliannol. Arhosodd Marconi gyda’n teulu yn y fferm wrth iddo ddatblygu radio. Mae cynghorwyr a’r plwyf yn Llandough yn gwrthod cydnabod hyn. Rwy’n deall bod Marconi yn cael ei ystyried yn wleidyddol eithafol ar y dde, ac, fel y gwelir yn achos y cerflun radio ym Mae Caerdydd, mae ei rôl hanesyddol yn cael ei hailysgrifennu. Mae’n rhesymol tybio bod ein teulu wedi cael ei ddal mewn ymgyrch wleidyddol ehangach o’r chwith yn erbyn y dde, ac mai am roi llety i Marconi y bu i ni wynebu canlyniadau canrif o hyd — problemau nad oedd yn bodoli yn y tair canrif flaenorol yr oeddem wedi byw ar y fferm.

Roedd mam Marconi hefyd yn Jamerson o gwmni wisgi Gwyddelig Jameson. Rwy’n gofyn i chi gynnal eich ymchwil eich hun, gwneud eich ymholiadau eich hun, a dod i’ch casgliadau eich hun — ond yn anad dim, peidiwch â chaniatáu i hanes gael ei ailysgrifennu yma.

Mae fy nheulu bellach yn archwilio opsiynau ar gyfer siarad cyhoeddus, hawliau stori, a dogfennaeth. Yn nhermau cysylltiadau teuluol: fy nhaid oedd Ray Smith o Dempsey and Makepeace; mae fy modryb yn Shan Cothi; a dechreuodd fy ewythr y band Tigertailz.

Rwy’n disgrifio’r sefyllfa hon fel gwarthus. Mae fy nheulu’n mynnu cyfiawnder am gael ein dadleoli a’n dwyn o’n tir a’n heiddo gan y Sefydliad Prydeinig a BP, gyda phrin unrhyw amddiffyniad dan y gyfraith. Rydym yn deulu Cymreig brodorol, Cymraeg eu hiaith, wedi byw yng Nghaerdydd, Bro Morgannwg, a’r fferm yn Llandough ers cannoedd o flynyddoedd.

O’r hyn y gallaf ei gasglu, ceir dwsinau o achosion posibl o dwyll a chuddio gwybodaeth, sy’n golygu nad yw statud cyfyngiadau yn berthnasol o reidrwydd. I’r rhai sy’n cefnogi dad-drefedigaethu Cymru ac annibyniaeth, prin y ceir enghraifft gliriach na BP v Buckler (1987) o’r hyn a ddigwyddodd i deulu ffermio Cymreig wrth herio’r Wladwriaeth Brydeinig a chorfforaeth fawr. Nid yw eraill wedi codi’r mater hwn, yn bennaf oherwydd trawma cenhedlaethol.

Rwyf wedi profi fy hun. Gadewais fy ngyrfa filwrol gydag anrhydedd, gan gwblhau fy llw 22 mlynedd. Cefais fy nghyflogi’n bona fide gan Gyngor Bro Morgannwg a Llywodraeth Cymru hyd at 2024. Gwasanaethais mewn rhyfeloedd yn y Dwyrain Canol. Fodd bynnag, nid yw’r anghyfiawnder fferm yn fater unigol.

Yn 2013, cafodd fy mab 36 diwrnod oed ei gipio, ac nid wyf erioed wedi ei weld ers hynny. Cafodd tŷ ei ddwyn oddi arnaf (40 Lombard Street, Y Barri). Yn 2023, cefais fy ngadael i gysgu mewn pabell tra roedd bron i 100 o Afghanistaniaid yn cael eu lletya’n dawel wrth ymyl ein pentref o 11 tŷ, tra roedd yn rhaid imi aros yno i ofalu am fy nain gan na allai gofalwyr ei chyrraedd.

O ganlyniad, rwyf bellach yn byw yn yr hyn a elwir yn Setliad Cymreig yn yr Ariannin. Rwyf wedi fy nisodli ac wedi fy dadleoli i’r eithaf. Serch hynny, rwy’n ddiolchgar fy mod wedi goroesi gyda’m rhyddid, fy mywyd, a’m henw da yn gymharol gyfan. Serch hynny, hoffwn fod wedi aros yng Nghymru, fel Cymro, gyda safon a chynhaliaeth bywyd deg.

Mae fy ngwraig a minnau’n amharod i ganiatáu i’n merch hyd yn oed gamu ar Ynysoedd Prydain o ystyried yr hyn a glywn sy’n digwydd yno. Yn 2024, allforiais hyd yn oed fy nghi o Abertawe i’n heiddo yn y Caribî ar ôl i unigolyn Afghanistan fod yng ngardd fy nheulu yng Nghymru, gan geisio ei ddwyn.

Gofynnaf i’r Senedd gymryd y mater hwn o ddifrif, ac ystyried sefydlu Ymchwiliad Cyhoeddus llawn, tryloyw ac annibynnol. Nid er budd fy nheulu yn unig y mae hyn, ond er uniondeb hanes, cyfiawnder tir, a hawliau dynol yng Nghymru.

Yn gywir,

Sion Buckler

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Sirs/Ma'am,

I am writing to you regarding a significant historical injustice involving my family, the Bucklers, and the destruction of Great House Farm (an 800-year-old site of monastic and Marconi history).

For example, in a 1974 press statement my grandmother said publically 'It's my home'—that directly contradicts the 1987 Court of Appeal ruling that she was 'silent' and accepted of BP license issued in 1974. My dad's appeal for the BP vs Buckler 1987 case also got dismissed on grounds both BP Pension Trust Ltd and BP Properties Ltd were effectively the same company. But in the ruling he was appealing, the judge said that my nans replies to BP Pensions Trust Ltd didn't count as BP Properties Ltd were the claimant, and the two were seperate companies. So it was heads they win, tails we lose. My dad was ripped from his hospital bed, jailed without charge and slapped with a restraining order to keep him from occupying and defending our 800 year old farm from being bulldozed down. His ECHR request blocked before he died in 1991 aged just 41.

I am requesting a Petition for a Public Inquiry into this case as a matter of historical land theft and human rights violations in Wales.

I'm a military cyber and electronic warfare professional. We all have very powerful AI technology at our disposal which can make light work out of all of this. My family suffered an incredible injustice. It also appears to be multi-generational warfare/ lawfare. Whereby we were treated as free labour to upkeep the asset of the land and property until it was ripe to be cashed in. I say this as every action against us seemed to be last minute.

There was allegedly press covering the 74 case and supporting my nan and family and farm. There was a petition of 1700 people trying to defend us and the farm from demolishment. CADW looked the other way when it should have been a Grade II listed building. I could go on and on and on.

I'm not even sure the land registry recorded that our land, being registered in 1982 by BP , was in dispute. I believe it was treated as if it wasn't dispited. No court actually definitively determined that BP were the landowners. It was just asserted.

Marconi stayed with our family at our farm when inventing radio. The councillors and parish at Llandough won't even acknowledge this. I understand Marconi was far right and so, like the radio statute at Cardiff Bay has confirmed, he is being re-written out of history.  It stands to reason that our family was caught in this political campaign of left vs right. And for helping Marconi we found ourselves experiencing a century of problems afterwards. Which didn't exist for the 3 centuries we were at our farm before letting far right marconi stay with us. Marconi's mother was also Jamerson of the Irish Whiskey company.

Do your own homework. Make your own enquiries. Draw your own conclusions.

 But please do not let history be rewritten here. My family are exploring options for public speaking, story rights, and a documentary etc.

My grandfather was Ray Smith, of Dempsey and Makepeace. My aunty Shan Cothi. My uncle started the band tigertailz.

This is an outrage and my family demands justice for being displaced and stolen from, land and property, by the British Establishment/ BP -  with little to no protections under law. And we're indigenous to the land, Welsh, Welsh speaking, Welsh family. Resident in Cardiff / Vale and that farm in Llandough for HUNDREDS OF YEARS.

There's tens of counts of fraud and concealment from what I can gather. Which means the statute of limitation doesn't apply in this instance. I know some are in favour of Wales decolonising and gaining independence. I think there's no better example of BP vs Buckler 1987 and what has happened to my family. Nobody else will bring this up because there's generational trauma. Notwithstanding we, a welsh farming family, are speaking up and against the British State and BP.

But I've proven myself. Leaving my military career with honours. Finishing my 22 years Oath, bona fide, employed by the Vale of Glamorgan Council, Welsh Government until 2024. I served in the wars in the middle east. I don't know what is going on, on that island. But the farm injustice isn't the only matter. My 36 day old son was abducted in 2013 and I've never seen him since. I had a house stolen (40 Lombard Street, Barry). And in 2023 I was left to sleep in a tent, while almost 100 afghans were secretly housed next to our 11 home village. Where I had to be to care for my grandmother, as no carers couldn't reach her. So I'm currently at the Welsh Settlement in Argentina. So I'm as displaced and replaced as I can be to cater for the insanity that's going on, on that island. And grateful I've managed to survive it all with my liberty and life and reputation somewhat still intact. But I would have actually liked to have remained in Wales as a Welshman. And have some quality and standard of life. My wife and I are reluctant for our daughter to even step foot on the British Isles with what we're hearing that's going on there lately. And I even exported my dog from Swansea to our place in the Caribbean in 2024 after an afghan was in my family's garden in Wales, trying to steal him.

I look forward to your reply,

Regards,

Sion Buckler

My intention is to place relevant public bodies on notice of a potential issue of public record integrity and heritage governance, not to obtain documents for private interest. I am therefore asking that my correspondence be treated as a formal expression of concern regarding the reliability and completeness of the archival record as it relates to this site, and that this concern be noted accordingly. I would also be grateful if you could advise which department or officer is appropriate for addressing concerns of this nature, where the issue is not access but potential historical misrepresentation within public records.

For the avoidance of doubt, I am not alleging any impropriety on the part of current archive staff. My concern relates to historical processes and decisions, and to ensuring that those matters are properly examined rather than inadvertently reinforced.

https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/archives-sector/finding-records-in-discovery-and-other-databases/manorial-documents-register/

        You don't often get email from [redacted]<mailto:[redacted]>. Learn why this is important <https://aka.ms/LearnAboutSenderIdentification>


EXTERNAL: This email originates from outside of The National Archives.

FORMAL NOTICE OF RECORD CHALLENGE, ASSERTION OF RIGHT, AND DEMAND FOR ENGAGEMENT

Dear Sir/Madam,

This Notice is issued for placement on official record and for reliance. It is not informal correspondence. I urge you not to resort to silence, deflection, or delay, as doing so following receipt of this notice constitutes knowing reliance upon, and maintenance of, records alleged to be materially defective through fraud, concealment, denial of due process, and systemic erasure. Please report any suspicious activity and discrepancies identified.

This Notice is issued in pursuit of narrative justice at this stage; formal judicial remedies are expressly reserved. It serves to document our family's side of the story before it is completely erased and history rewritten, ensuring awareness among custodians of land, heritage, heraldry, archaeology, and public records.

My elder brother, Rhys Buckler, and I are the sons of the late William Buckler (d. 1991), defendant in the landmark legal case BP Properties Ltd v Buckler (1987), and the grandchildren of the late Mary Williams, whose dispossession, marginalisation, and exclusion from judicial determination remain unresolved matters of record. Mary Williams was repeatedly and materially falsely addressed/mislabeled in legal and administrative records as "Mrs Buckler," a misidentification that was never judicially tested and which directly affected the handling, scope, and outcome of proceedings. The Williams/Buckler family held claim to the land title, having acquired and occupied Great House Farm continuously since 1667, based on family records, historical evidence, and centuries of resistance to adverse claims.

I place on record that I am the first member of my family able to speak publicly and formally on these matters. Other close family members remain too traumatised and intimidated by the historical conduct of these proceedings-including violent eviction, demolition, and loss of livelihood-to engage, despite the continuing consequences of dispossession. That silence must not be misread as consent, acquiescence, or abandonment of right. There is a material distinction between free silence and silence produced by fear, trauma, and coercive experience.

The story, as we have pieced it together, reveals a multi-generational pattern of lawfare and siege: from Norman/English conquests in 1100 granting lordships over ancient Welsh Christian landscapes, through monastic (1215-1539) and Crown seizures (1539 onward), to industrial encroachments (e.g., 1876 Limeworks severance without consent) and modern corporate possession actions. This culminated in the 1988 demolition of an 800-year-old farmhouse amid police standoffs, leaving the family homeless and the site scarred, now buried under Church View Close. Archaeological vindication came too late-1994 excavations revealed over 1,000 Roman and medieval burials, confirming family warnings (e.g., the 1870 Roman soldier discovery under the living room floor, suppressed by authorities)-yet heritage records celebrate the site while omitting our dispossession.

The following assertions of right are now formally placed on record. They have never been lawfully adjudicated or extinguished:

1.      Rhys Buckler may be the rightful Manorial Lord of the Manor of Llandough, by right of primogeniture and continuous hereditary connection arising from our family's occupation of Great House Farm from 1667 until our narrative, legal, and physical dispossession.
2.      I assert a claim to act as Squire of the Manor of Llandough, as executive representative and guardian of the Buckler-Williams estate and matriarchal lineage, with a mandate to pursue correction of record, restitution, and restorative remedies.

These are assertions of right, not settled declarations, placed on record pending proper adjudication-which has been historically obstructed through procedural narrowing, missing documents, and avoidance of full hearings.

In 1974, Mary Williams was twice prevented from presenting her case and obtaining a judicial determination of superior ownership, despite claims grounded in long occupation, intent, and possession. The court confined inquiry to animus possidendi (intention to possess) and excluded animus domini (intention to own), reclassifying her from putative owner to mere occupier and foreclosing title adjudication. BP sought possession only, not ownership rulings-a choice unexplained and significant. Proceedings were adjourned or quashed without resolution.

This occurred despite evidence of ownership intent, including:

*       Centuries-long occupation and resistance (e.g., failed 1938 auction due to local support; post-1945 rent disputes).
*       Roman-era remains and historical significance (e.g., Guglielmo Marconi's 1897 residence during radio experiments, with family aid erased from records).
*       Unformalized deals like the 1895-1905 Daniel Thomas quarrying permission for promised title, undermined by vanished deeds.

Judicial ownership examination would have engaged archaeological/heritage protections, incompatible with redevelopment-consequences avoided, raising credibility concerns.

Serious unresolved anomalies persist, indicating something is still not right with the record:

*       Licence correspondence dated 31 October 1974 surfacing only on 4 November, potentially interrupting proceedings to prevent hearings.
*       Claims of 1974 benevolent withdrawal under press scrutiny unsupported by verifiable coverage.
*       Land registration before Mary Williams's 1983 death without title determination; disputes possibly lodged/suppressed by Land Registry.
*       Inconsistent treatment of BP entities across proceedings to family detriment.
*       Procedural barriers preventing effective defense (e.g., interrupted essential services post-licence; 1960-1987 court rulings dismissing ancestral title as "notion" without evidence).
*       Knowing bypass of archaeological constraints (e.g., 1978 trenches ignored; no contemporaneous 1970s/1990s press on discoveries amid development).
*       Missing key documents (e.g., 1667 conveyance, 1811-1835 Lambert Williams agreements proving status, 1982-84 library deeds vanishing).
*       Risks of further erasure: Heritage databases celebrate "Llandough Roman villa cemetery" while omitting our saga; modern residents unaware of the "battleground" site.

These anomalies suggest systemic theft, from colonial English subjugation (e.g., 1543-1770 orbit shifts) to corporate siege, during Wales' cultural/economic transitions. Authority derived through such means is illegitimate under natural justice, customary Welsh principles, and moral-legal frameworks. The record's distortion secures advantage, but passage of time does not validate it.

Preliminary assessment indicates cumulative benefits from redevelopment (absent title extinguishment) exceed £100 million, forming a basis for reparations-covering lost land, artifacts, livelihood, and trauma.

I require relevant public servants, custodians, and office-holders (including Land Registry, heraldry bodies, museums, archaeologists, MPs, historians, and councillors) to cease delay, engage substantively, review/correct/annotate records where defective, and prevent further rewriting of history. Justice delayed is denied, especially with verifiable evidence available.

This Notice:

*       Challenges the record's accuracy, completeness, and legitimacy.
*       Place assertions of title/standing on record pending adjudication.
*       Reserves all rights without prejudice.
*       Puts officials/beneficiaries on notice that silence/reliance may aggravate responsibility.

For the avoidance of doubt, His Majesty the King was notified yesterday.

This serves as an invitation to engage constructively before reliance becomes untenable.

Regards, Requester On behalf of the Buckler-Williams family [redacted], Wales. https://bpvsbuckler.datro.xyz/ <https://bpvsbuckler.datro.xyz/>

Postscript - Disability and Succession (Material Notice): The heir-apparent to the asserted Manorial Lordship is Rhys Buckler's son, a young man with Down syndrome. Any obstruction, marginalisation, or differential treatment affecting his inheritance would engage the Equality Act 2010 and UK international obligations on disability rights. Disability cannot bar succession or recognition. This is recorded to prevent claims of ignorance.

Dear Mr Gale,

Thank you for your reply of 12 February. I would like to clarify and narrow
my request to ensure there is no misunderstanding regarding the records I
am trying to locate.

My correspondence is *not* seeking an adjudication of ownership or title —
I fully accept the stated remit boundaries of the Manorial Documents
Register (MDR). Rather, my enquiry concerns the existence of *any archival
reference, index card, catalogue entry, or pointer to a document
historically known as the “Williams Title”*, which was, according to
contemporaneous family testimony, at one point:

   1.

   Held in the *local public library* in the first half of the twentieth
   century; and
   2.

   Indexed in some manner (e.g., an index card or catalogue reference) that
   persisted even after the original document could not be located.

My understanding of the MDR — as described on your own website — is that it
exists to provide brief descriptions of manorial records and details of
their locations:

“An official index of English and Welsh manorial records providing brief
descriptions of documents and details of their locations… It does *not*
include title deeds or conveyances, and is *not* a register of ownership of
manorial lordships or rights.”
https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/manor-search
<https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/manor-search?utm_source=chatgpt.com>

Based on that description, I would be grateful if you could confirm whether:

   1.

   *Any catalogue entries, index cards, reference pointers, or archival
   descriptions* relating to the *Manor of Llandough* or the *Williams
   family title* exist in the MDR or related archival catalogues.
   2.

   If so, the *reference identifiers* and information on how these can be
   consulted in person or via digitised records.

To be precise, I am looking for historical references to the *index card or
listing* for the Williams Title — whether held in a library, local record
office, or other institutional archive — rather than a claim for ownership
judgment itself.

If such a reference does not currently appear in the MDR, I would greatly
appreciate guidance on where any known catalogue cards or entry lists for
manorial documents from *Glamorgan / Llandough* prior to 1950 might now
reside (e.g., regional archives, National Archives holdings, or affiliated
local repository catalogues).

Anyway I anticipate your forgiveness, if I have erred in writing to you
earlier.

Thank you again and in advance for your assistance.

Yours sincerely,


Sion Buckler

Dear Mr Buckler.

Thank you for your email.

Glamorgan Archives had at one time a large number of paper catalogues, along with card indexes.  The data from these was transferred into our catalogue when we moved from analogue to digital.  The original catalogues and cards were not retained.

Our catalogue only records descriptions of documents that are held within our collection.  If a document is permanently withdrawn from the collection, we would remove the description from the catalogue. Many of our records are private records held on deposit on behalf of the owner.  We have no control over what they do or don’t give us.  The owner retains the right to withdraw these documents if they wish.

In that context, I am not seeking to pay for copies of records whose accuracy is itself in question, nor to participate financially in processes that may inadvertently perpetuate errors arising from that period. My intention is to place relevant public bodies on notice of a potential issue of public record integrity and heritage governance, not to obtain documents for private interest. I am therefore asking that my correspondence be treated as a formal expression of concern regarding the reliability and completeness of the archival record as it relates to this site, and that this concern be noted accordingly. I would also be grateful if you could advise which department or officer is appropriate for addressing concerns of this nature, where the issue is not access but potential historical misrepresentation within public records.

For the avoidance of doubt, I am not alleging any impropriety on the part of current archive staff. My concern relates to historical processes and decisions, and to ensuring that those matters are properly examined rather than inadvertently reinforced.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Yours sincerely,

FORMAL NOTICE OF RECORD CHALLENGE, ASSERTION OF RIGHT, AND DEMAND FOR ENGAGEMENT



Dear Sir/Madam,



This Notice is issued for placement on official record and for reliance. It is not informal correspondence. I urge you not to resort to silence, deflection, or delay, as doing so following receipt of this notice constitutes knowing reliance upon, and maintenance of, records alleged to be materially defective through fraud, concealment, denial of due process, and systemic erasure. Please report any suspicious activity and discrepancies identified.



This Notice is issued in pursuit of narrative justice at this stage; formal judicial remedies are expressly reserved. It serves to document our family's side of the story before it is completely erased and history rewritten, ensuring awareness among custodians of land, heritage, heraldry, archaeology, and public records.



My elder brother, Rhys Buckler, and I are the sons of the late William Buckler (d. 1991), defendant in the landmark legal case BP Properties Ltd v Buckler (1987), and the grandchildren of the late Mary Williams, whose dispossession, marginalisation, and exclusion from judicial determination remain unresolved matters of record. Mary Williams was repeatedly and materially falsely addressed/mislabeled in legal and administrative records as “Mrs Buckler,” a misidentification that was never judicially tested and which directly affected the handling, scope, and outcome of proceedings. The Williams/Buckler family held claim to the land title, having acquired and occupied Great House Farm continuously since 1667, based on family records, historical evidence, and centuries of resistance to adverse claims.



I place on record that I am the first member of my family able to speak publicly and formally on these matters. Other close family members remain too traumatised and intimidated by the historical conduct of these proceedings—including violent eviction, demolition, and loss of livelihood—to engage, despite the continuing consequences of dispossession. That silence must not be misread as consent, acquiescence, or abandonment of right. There is a material distinction between free silence and silence produced by fear, trauma, and coercive experience.



The story, as we have pieced it together, reveals a multi-generational pattern of lawfare and siege: from Norman/English conquests in 1100 granting lordships over ancient Welsh Christian landscapes, through monastic (1215–1539) and Crown seizures (1539 onward), to industrial encroachments (e.g., 1876 Limeworks severance without consent) and modern corporate possession actions. This culminated in the 1988 demolition of an 800-year-old farmhouse amid police standoffs, leaving the family homeless and the site scarred, now buried under Church View Close. Archaeological vindication came too late—1994 excavations revealed over 1,000 Roman and medieval burials, confirming family warnings (e.g., the 1870 Roman soldier discovery under the living room floor, suppressed by authorities)—yet heritage records celebrate the site while omitting our dispossession.



The following assertions of right are now formally placed on record. They have never been lawfully adjudicated or extinguished:



1.      Rhys Buckler may be the rightful Manorial Lord of the Manor of Llandough, by right of primogeniture and continuous hereditary connection arising from our family’s occupation of Great House Farm from 1667 until our narrative, legal, and physical dispossession.

2.      I assert a claim to act as Squire of the Manor of Llandough, as executive representative and guardian of the Buckler–Williams estate and matriarchal lineage, with a mandate to pursue correction of record, restitution, and restorative remedies.



These are assertions of right, not settled declarations, placed on record pending proper adjudication—which has been historically obstructed through procedural narrowing, missing documents, and avoidance of full hearings.



In 1974, Mary Williams was twice prevented from presenting her case and obtaining a judicial determination of superior ownership, despite claims grounded in long occupation, intent, and possession. The court confined inquiry to animus possidendi (intention to possess) and excluded animus domini (intention to own), reclassifying her from putative owner to mere occupier and foreclosing title adjudication. BP sought possession only, not ownership rulings—a choice unexplained and significant. Proceedings were adjourned or quashed without resolution.



This occurred despite evidence of ownership intent, including:



*       Centuries-long occupation and resistance (e.g., failed 1938 auction due to local support; post-1945 rent disputes).

*       Roman-era remains and historical significance (e.g., Guglielmo Marconi's 1897 residence during radio experiments, with family aid erased from records).

*       Unformalized deals like the 1895–1905 Daniel Thomas quarrying permission for promised title, undermined by vanished deeds.



Judicial ownership examination would have engaged archaeological/heritage protections, incompatible with redevelopment—consequences avoided, raising credibility concerns.



Serious unresolved anomalies persist, indicating something is still not right with the record:



*       Licence correspondence dated 31 October 1974 surfacing only on 4 November, potentially interrupting proceedings to prevent hearings.

*       Claims of 1974 benevolent withdrawal under press scrutiny unsupported by verifiable coverage.

*       Land registration before Mary Williams’s 1983 death without title determination; disputes possibly lodged/suppressed by Land Registry.

*       Inconsistent treatment of BP entities across proceedings to family detriment.

*       Procedural barriers preventing effective defense (e.g., interrupted essential services post-licence; 1960–1987 court rulings dismissing ancestral title as "notion" without evidence).

*       Knowing bypass of archaeological constraints (e.g., 1978 trenches ignored; no contemporaneous 1970s/1990s press on discoveries amid development).

*       Missing key documents (e.g., 1667 conveyance, 1811–1835 Lambert Williams agreements proving status, 1982–84 library deeds vanishing).

*       Risks of further erasure: Heritage databases celebrate "Llandough Roman villa cemetery" while omitting our saga; modern residents unaware of the "battleground" site.



These anomalies suggest systemic theft, from colonial English subjugation (e.g., 1543–1770 orbit shifts) to corporate siege, during Wales' cultural/economic transitions. Authority derived through such means is illegitimate under natural justice, customary Welsh principles, and moral-legal frameworks. The record's distortion secures advantage, but passage of time does not validate it.



Preliminary assessment indicates cumulative benefits from redevelopment (absent title extinguishment) exceed £100 million, forming a basis for reparations—covering lost land, artifacts, livelihood, and trauma.



I require relevant public servants, custodians, and office-holders (including Land Registry, heraldry bodies, museums, archaeologists, MPs, historians, and councillors) to cease delay, engage substantively, review/correct/annotate records where defective, and prevent further rewriting of history. Justice delayed is denied, especially with verifiable evidence available.



This Notice:



*       Challenges the record's accuracy, completeness, and legitimacy.

*       Place assertions of title/standing on record pending adjudication.

*       Reserves all rights without prejudice.

*       Puts officials/beneficiaries on notice that silence/reliance may aggravate responsibility.



For the avoidance of doubt, His Majesty the King was notified yesterday.



This serves as an invitation to engage constructively before reliance becomes untenable.



Regards, Requester On behalf of the Buckler–Williams family [redacted], Wales. https://bpvsbuckler.datro.xyz/ <https://bpvsbuckler.datro.xyz/>



Postscript — Disability and Succession (Material Notice): The heir-apparent to the asserted Manorial Lordship is Rhys Buckler’s son, a young man with Down syndrome. Any obstruction, marginalisation, or differential treatment affecting his inheritance would engage the Equality Act 2010 and UK international obligations on disability rights. Disability cannot bar succession or recognition. This is recorded to prevent claims of ignorance.

Dear Requester,

Thank you for your email regarding Great House Farm, Llandough. However, I must inform you that much of the content in your correspondence falls outside the scope of Cadw’s work.

In relation to the claim of 'archaeological suppression' involving the discovery of a Roman soldier in full armour in 1888, any such find would typically have been reported in the antiquarian press at either the national or local level. It is possible that records of this nature may be held by local museums. It is worth noting that the first Ancient Monuments Act was passed in 1882, focusing solely on bringing threatened ancient monuments into guardianship. The legal recognition of nationally important archaeology did not come about until the Ancient Monuments Consolidation and Amendment Act of 1913.

Upon reviewing the Cof Cymru database, I found that there are no designated historic assets relevant to this topic. However, Archwilio contains two records that document the involvement of the Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust (GGAT):

1. Great House Farm HER site entry - GGAT03586s
2. Land at Great House Farm HER event entry - GGATE003872, which includes GGAT's 1990 archaeological assessment report commissioned by BP Properties Ltd.

Any advice or correspondence that Cadw may have provided should be preserved in the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales (RCAHMW) National Monuments Record of Wales (NMRW). I recommend you contact the NMRW to access any relevant documents. Additionally, you may want to reach out to Heneb and the Vale of Glamorgan Local Planning Authority (LPA) to explore what records they might hold concerning this matter.

Kind regards,

Jenna Arnold

Subject: Formal Report of Suspected Indigenous Dispossession, Systemic Fraud, and Archaeological Suppression – Great House Farm, Llandough


To whom it may concern,

I am writing to formally report a long-standing and systemic case of what I suspect may be dispossession, fraudulent misrepresentation, and archaeological suppression concerning my family’s ancestral land, Great House Farm (historically Tŷ Mawr/Cedfin), Llandough.

I am the descendant of the Williams/Buckler family, who held de facto possession and indigenous tenure of this land from 1667 until our forced displacement in 1988. I am currently the only member of my family who is not too traumatized to speak of these events. My mother (Mary Williams daughter in law), remains to this day too terrified to speak up about this multi-generational "lawfare" campaign waged against us. Our family have not seen justice or received reperations, nor have we sued or reopened this case under limitations act clauses of fraud and consealment. Yet. But this may not be just a grave injustice upon our family, but our nations archeological history and indigenous people on our ancestral birthland. We are Welsh Nationals, Welsh speaking, under Welsh flags. This is some British Colonisation-grade trespass I'm seeing and it's tandamount to a declaration of civil war on me, my family, community and people.

The core of this report involves the following suspicions I have of concealment and fraud (see attached for my timeline and notes):

  1.  Archaeological Suppression: In 1888, my family discovered a Roman soldier in full armor beneath the living room floorboards. This discovery provided "actual notice" of the site's national significance a century before its demolition. We allege this notice was systematically suppressed by corporate and state actors to allow for commercial development.
  2.  Fraudulent Misrepresentation in Planning: During the 1987 planning process, the 13th-century fortified manor was described by developers as a "dilapidated utility building" or "ruined barn" to secure a demolition permit that would have otherwise been denied under heritage protection laws.
  3.  Legal Identity Falsification: In 1974, BP Pension Trust issued a "unilateral license" intended to bypass our possessory title. This correspondence was falsely addressed to "Mrs. Buckler" to bind my grandmother to her deceased husband’s name and legal status, despite her public rejection of their claim. She used her maiden name Williams and her husband Bucklers' intent to accept license died with him. My nan also alledgedly didn't expressly deny the offer and so accepted through her silence. But she was near enough voiceless from screaming for decades that she will not do deals with any of them. That's a different kind of silence, if any. And to have responded to license to Mrs Buckler would have been identify fraud as she was Mrs Williams. And she did in fact reject BPs license offer and advanced, countless times, but publically. I believe these objections were suppressed too. There's allegedly news coverage from October 30th 1974 but I'm yet to find the evidence. But see attached a 1978 article I unearthed. My nan clearly maintains her position "It's my home". [cid:image004.jpg@01DCA64B.15168E30]
  4.  You'll also see in landmark legal case BP Vs Buckler 1987 the judge says that she might have responded to BP, but to BP Pension Trust, but the claimant was BP Properties Ltd which were two separate companies. But in my dads appeal when he challenges that BP Pension Trust Ltd should have been the claimant the same judge dismissed his appeal citing both BP companies are effectively the same. This is clearly a case of heads BP won, Tails we lost.
  5.  Missing Evidence: Critical title deeds and Bute Estate records from our families deal with Daniel Thomas, for title after quarrying completed, in exchange for our permission to quarry, also disappeared from the loft of our home and the Cardiff Library according to my families accounts, precisely when they were needed to support our ownership claim in the Court of Appeal. Regardless we should have still remained on grounds we'd been there since 1667, and failing that on grounds of adverse possession.
  6.  It was evident lawfare to remove us, to get to the burials known about since 1888, BP profited from the land sale, the state and Crown have the exhevated artifacts and my displaced family are left traumatised, cheated and dead. My dad's appeal was dismissed to when it shouldn't have been and his ECHR request blocked, before dying abruptly at age just 41.

The confirmation in 1994 of a high-status Roman villa and over 1,000 burials on the exact site of our demolished home proves that the "official narrative" used to evict us was predicated on the concealment of known facts.

Under Section 32 of the Limitation Act 1980, the limitation period for action does not begin until such fraud or concealment is discovered. As the heir to this possessory title, I am seeking a formal investigation into the institutional failures that permitted this dispossession and the destruction of a national monument.

I have compiled my account and understanding of these events in timeline order and I'm prepared to provide further testimony and evidence.

Given the extreme trauma my family has suffered, I request that all correspondence be handled with the gravity this human rights violation deserves.

Considering the lack of cooperation from my traumatised family. And authorities who maybe complicit and implicated. And possible corruption of records and fraud and consealment, I'm open to the fact my account and understanding may not be perfect. But if even a single other person or group looked into this too, even briefly, I'm sure you'll agree there's merrit to the concerns I'm raising with all of this.

I look forward to your response regarding the appropriate next steps for investigation and restitution.

I do ask for some small sense of urgency in that justice delayed is justice denied. I understand this is ancient news for many, but my family still feel a tremendous sense of disposition and disposition over all of this. Bringing this all up means to re live it.

I will have been 3 or 4 at the time, but I still remember my toys in our house, being bulldozed. And my mum handing us rocks to throw at them, bulldozing down our home. As my dad was held without charges to prevent him defending us and our home. I'd have to visit him in a hospital bed after his heart attack and see him in a coffin shortly afterwards.

I'm 41 years old now. I'm a certified and experienced military commander and leader. I left my military career with honours. I finished 22 years in Oath in 2024, bond afide, my last 2 employed under the Welsh government.

I kindly request but also require of you, that this matter be layed to rest correctly.

Dear Mr Buckler,

Thank you for your e-mail and for clarifying the subject of your enquiry.
